title_en: GM108: Maybe Japan Is Finally Changing for Real ft. Jesper Koll
title_zh: GM108：日本这次或许真的在改变（对话 Jesper Koll）
subtitle_zh: Jesper Koll 认为，日本正站在 30 年来的第一个拐点上：企业治理、薪酬体系与股东回报都在改变，资本开始回流国内。他逐一拆解债务、人口结构、日元与日本央行（BOJ）正常化，论证这轮转变并非依赖 AI，而是源自产业整合与扎实的基本功。结论是——日本或许真的在发生结构性转变，而现在是看多日本资产的良机。

turns.zh: 我状态好极了，谢谢你们邀请我。太好了。是这样，正如我们在开始录音前我跟你说的，我关注你的工作已经很久了，差不多和我入行的时间一样长，而那已经是相当长的一段时间了。所以，能和你交谈、听你聊聊

turns.zh: 日本正在发生的种种事情，是一件很愉快的事。你最初是怎么对经济学、市场、尤其是日本产生兴趣的？嗯，其实非常简单。我原本是德国人，后来拿到奖学金去一所国际寄宿学校读书。我学的是数学，之后参与进了 OECD，

turns.en: I've never left the country. After learning Japanese and staying a little bit at Kyoto University, I got a job working for a Japanese Member of Parliament. And I ended up doing that and staying there for about three years and then got pushed or pulled, at the peak of the bubble, into financial markets. First
turns.zh: 我从没离开过这个国家。学了日语、又在 Kyoto University 待了一小段时间之后，我找了一份工作，给一位日本国会议员做事。结果我一干就是大约三年，然后在泡沫的顶峰，半推半就地被拉进了金融市场。先是

turns.zh: 在赫赫有名的 S.G. Warburg，然后是 J.P. Morgan，接着在 Tiger Fund 跟着 Julian Robertson 干了一阵，再到 Merrill Lynch、JP Morgan，如今我在 Manx Group 工作。我们在日本有一只小型的激进主义基金，我同时还是另外几只基金的顾问，也是东京都知事的顾问，偶尔还

turns.en: Great stuff. Well, that's a great background. Clearly, you're very embedded in everything from an economic perspective, from a policy, from a markets perspective. And I know you are now known as the Japan Optimist. So maybe that's a good starting point. I mean, as you often say in your podcasts and videos, there's
turns.zh: 太好了。嗯，这是一段很棒的履历。显然，无论从经济、政策还是市场的角度，你都深度嵌入其中。我知道你现在以 Japan Optimist 著称。所以这也许是个不错的切入点。正如你在播客和视频里常说的，围绕日本有

turns.en: a lot of pessimism around Japan. So, what's the optimistic case? Look, I mean, it's actually interesting, Alan, because I started the Japan Optimist, actually when I was at J.P. Morgan, and this was early, when Japan was sinking into a deflationary pit. And everybody from Paul Krugman to Larry Summers had these
turns.zh: 很多悲观情绪。那么，乐观的理由是什么？你看，这其实很有意思，Alan，因为我开始做 Japan Optimist，其实是在 J.P. Morgan 的时候，那是很早以前，当时日本正陷入通缩（deflation）的泥潭。从 Paul Krugman 到 Larry Summers，每个人都给出了这些

turns.en: great pieces of advice on what to do. And basically, anybody who's been in Japan who sticks around, who visits Japanese companies and talks to the policymakers, this is an incredibly organized methodological place. They don't talk a lot, but they analyze a lot and they act
turns.zh: 关于该怎么做的绝妙建议。而基本上，任何一个待在日本、愿意留下来、去拜访日本企业、和政策制定者交谈的人都会发现，这是一个极其有条理、极其讲方法的地方。他们话不多，但会做大量分析，而且行动

turns.en: very methodologically. And I just thought, like, look, if everybody's pessimistic, this is the right time to give Japan a little bit of a boost. And as you know, the Japanese don't really speak out. Whether you go to Davos or whether you go to any international conference, there's hardly anybody who sort of speaks up for
turns.zh: 非常有方法。我当时就想，你看，如果所有人都悲观，那正是给日本加把劲、鼓鼓劲的时候。你也知道，日本人其实不太发声。无论你是去 Davos，还是去任何国际会议，几乎没有人站出来为

turns.en: Japan. But the reality, whether it's from macroeconomics… I mean, just simple reality, that even throughout the 1990s and early, when Japan was at risk of falling into deflation, Japan continued to be the world's largest creditor country. And the fact that Japan continues year in, year out, to generate record
turns.zh: 日本说话。但现实是——无论从宏观经济看，还是仅仅从朴素的事实看——即便在整个 1990 年代以及更早、日本面临陷入通缩风险的那段时期，日本始终是全球最大的债权国。而且日本年复一年地创造出创纪录的

turns.en: balance of payments surpluses just tells you that there's an enormous strength that Japan actually brings to the table. And right now it's very interesting because obviously Japan is not at all in the game of artificial intelligence, but Japan is very much in the game of physical AI actually translating virtual intelligence
turns.zh: 国际收支顺差（balance of payments surplus），这就说明日本实际上带来了一种巨大的实力。而现在这一点非常有意思，因为显然日本完全没有参与人工智能（AI）这场竞赛，但日本却深深参与了物理 AI（physical AI）这场竞赛，也就是把虚拟的智能

turns.en: into the analog world, into the real world. The Japanese manufacturing companies have what it takes. They've got the intellectual property. Japan never abandoned its focus on the world class engineering.
turns.zh: 转化到模拟世界、转化到现实世界。日本的制造企业具备所需的一切。他们拥有知识产权。而如今日元走弱，日本在全球市场上变得非常、非常有竞争力。所以，这是回归基本面的根本优势。日本从未放弃对世界级工程技术的专注。

turns.en: And that's now where Japan is going to be a key beneficiary of what's going on in the world.
turns.zh: 而这，正是日本将成为当下世界变局中一个关键受益者的地方。

I mean obviously, the demographic scenario has resulted in lower GDP growth, but
turns.zh: 有意思。人们谈论日本时通常会提到两大逆风：债务和人口结构。你已经稍微谈到了人口结构，但也许可以再讲讲这两点，以及你怎么看它们的走向。显然，人口结构的局面导致了更低的 GDP 增长，但

I mean that's enormous. And obviously there's a drag on national income, on GDP that's going to come from that. But this is not what you
turns.zh: 经济体。你看……日本人的平均年龄现在是 50 岁。你在经济史上第一次见到这样一个社会：每三个人中就有一个靠养老金生活。这是极其庞大的数字。显然，这会给国民收入、给 GDP 带来拖累。但这并不是你

turns.en: and I make our living with. You and I make our living by investing in number one, macroeconomic dynamics and number two, into individual corporations. turns.en: motivation, internal incentives. Anybody in the audience who's ever dealt with a Japanese company, the first thing that you notice is that they are unbelievably proud. I mean they are engineers, they are craftsmen, they want to build the best car, the best speed reducer. And changing on a dime is
turns.zh: 动力和内部激励机制的催化剂。在座任何跟日本公司打过交道的人，你首先会注意到的一点是，他们极其自尊、极其自豪。他们是工程师、是工匠，他们想造出最好的汽车、最好的减速器（speed reducer）。而要他们来了个一百八十度大转弯，

turns.en: not something that comes through them. Just changing their behavior now is being forced upon them. Because even a company like Mitsubishi, which is the JP Morgan or the gold standard here in Japan, even a company like Mitsubishi Corporation has to fight to retain its most important asset, which is human capital. So,
turns.zh: 并不是他们与生俱来的本领。如今他们行为的改变，是被逼出来的。因为哪怕像 Mitsubishi 这样的公司——它是日本的 JP Morgan，是这里的黄金标准——哪怕像 Mitsubishi Corporation 这样的公司，也必须为留住它最重要的资产、也就是人力资本（human capital）而奋力争取。所以，

turns.en: as a result of that you're finding that incredible things are happening. I mean Japan, the compensation system as many of you know, was basically seniority based pay. And as a result of that, everybody was very risk averse. As long as I don't screw up, I will stay on the escalator and will continue to get
turns.zh: 结果就是，你会发现一些不可思议的事情正在发生。日本过去的薪酬体系，很多人知道，基本上是论资排辈的薪酬（seniority-based pay）。因此所有人都非常规避风险。只要我不把事情搞砸，我就能一直站在自动扶梯上，继续拿到

turns.en: my pay increases every other year. Now, leading companies, like NTT, which is one of the most unionized companies in Japan, they're introducing pay for performance, they're introducing meritocracy. And the reason for this is this scarcity of labor. And that's why I'm very, very bullish on Japan, because it's a
turns.zh: 每隔一年一次的加薪。如今，像 NTT 这样的领先企业——它是日本工会化程度最高的公司之一——正在引入绩效薪酬（pay for performance）、引入择优制。原因就在于劳动力的这种稀缺。这也是为什么我对日本非常、非常看好，因为它是一个

turns.en: very rich country, as I mentioned, world's largest creditor country, it's a very proud country. But now your most important asset, which is human capital, you're running out of it. And therefore, how do I incentivize it, how do I retain the labor, becomes a big, big issue. And that's where productivity growth is going
turns.zh: 非常富裕的国家，正如我提到的，全球最大的债权国，也是一个非常自尊的国家。但如今你最重要的资产——人力资本——正在枯竭。因此，我该如何激励它、如何留住劳动力，就成了一个非常重大的问题。而生产率的增长，将

turns.zh: 正来源于此。它不会来自 AI，因为任何人都能买到 AI。问题在于，你如何激励你的团队？而这正是日本正在发生的变化。这也是为什么你会想对日本非常、非常看好。

turns.en: Okay, interesting. Well, the other factor then is debt. And obviously that's the, I suppose, Japan has been the poster child for rising debt levels and unsustainable debt and how the world's going to come to an end because of these high debt levels, but obviously it hasn't happened. JGB yields have gone up considerably, but to

turns.zh: 目前为止，它似乎还是可控的。你对这一点怎么看？显然，等式的另一边还有资产端。分析师们是不是有点误解了局面，还是说日本确实存在债务问题？不，答案是不存在债务问题。我是说，如果日本……

turns.en: I mean, people talk about the Liz Truss moment coming any day now. I'm sorry, the UK runs balance of payments deficits. That's when you have a problem because you need to fight to attract capital. Japan has excess capital. Japanese banks have excess deposits. They don't know what to do with their money. I'm exaggerating
turns.zh: 人们总在说 Liz Truss 时刻随时会到来。抱歉，英国是国际收支逆差。那才是你有麻烦的时候，因为你必须奋力去吸引资本。日本有超额资本。日本的银行有超额存款。他们不知道该怎么处理自己的钱。我说得有点夸张

turns.en: a little bit, right? But I mean, the reality of debt… And it's funny because I'm almost embarrassed because as a German national, I'm not supposed to think this way. But I always accuse people. It's like, why do you focus only on the liability side? The reality is that for every 100 yen of public debt taken on over the last
turns.zh: 了，对吧？但我是说，债务的现实……这很有趣，因为我几乎觉得不好意思，因为作为一个德国人，我本不该这样想。但我总是质问人们：你们为什么只盯着负债端？现实是，在过去

turns.en: 20 years, the private sector has generated 140 yen of savings. And these savings are stuck on corporate balance sheets, which are very lazy. There's a lot of cash that Japanese corporations have been hoarding. And on top of that you've got Mr. and Mrs. Watanabe where year in, year out you've got very, very high household sector
turns.zh: 20 年里，每承担 100 日元的公共债务，私人部门就产生了 140 日元的储蓄。而这些储蓄被困在企业资产负债表上，这些资产负债表非常“懒惰”。日本企业一直在囤积大量现金。除此之外，你还有 Watanabe 夫妇（Mr. and Mrs. Watanabe，指日本散户投资者），他们年复一年地保持着非常高的家庭部门

turns.en: net savings rates. So, the debt I don't think is a problem. It's a problem for the government because of course your budget allocation increasingly is being taken up by expense. Prime Minister Takaichi now basically has to spend, give or take, just shy of one quarter of her budget to service debt. And of course,
turns.zh: 净储蓄率。所以，我认为债务不是问题。它对政府来说是个问题，因为你的预算分配越来越多地被开支占据。Takaichi 首相现在基本上必须拿出预算中将近四分之一来偿还债务。当然，

turns.en: if interest rates go up, you've got a sensitivity that makes that more stringent. So, the politicians are up in arms because their, as it were, disposable spending is being curtailed. But it's not a problem for the macro economy because as I said, net, net. I'm a surplus saver in the macroeconomic sense.
turns.zh: 如果利率上升，那种敏感性会让局面更加紧张。所以政客们跳脚，因为他们可自由支配的开支正在被削减。但这对宏观经济不是问题，因为正如我说的，净而又净地看，我在宏观经济意义上是个净储蓄者。

turns.en: Okay, where are those savings now going? Obviously yields have gone from… 30-year yields have gone from 0% to 4% or so. So, clearly… Is a reluctance domestically to buy government bonds? Obviously the GPIF have trillions and trillions of dollars too. I mean there's been this general sense, obviously the carry trade
turns.zh: 好的，那么这些储蓄现在流向了哪里？显然收益率已经从……30 年期收益率已经从 0% 升到了 4% 左右。所以，很明显……国内是不是不愿意买国债？显然 GPIF 也持有数万亿美元。我是说，一直有这样一个普遍感觉，显然套息交易（carry trade）

turns.en: is there, that a lot of Japan's capital has been going overseas. As you say, it's a creditor to the rest of the world. Give us your perspective on that. What has happened and what is likely to happen going forward. No, Alan. And now you are hitting what's really relevant because
turns.zh: 是存在的，日本有大量资本一直在流向海外。正如你所说，它是世界其他地区的债权人。给我们讲讲你对这一点的看法。已经发生了什么，接下来又可能发生什么。不，Alan。你现在正触及真正关键的地方，因为

turns.en: I do think that we are at an inflection point for the first time in 30 years. Over the last 30 years because the domestic returns were in fixed income land basically kept at close to zero. On top of that you had corporate managers basically preferring to hoard cash and build lazy balance sheet rather than raising
turns.zh: 我确实认为，我们正处于 30 年来的第一个拐点。过去 30 年里，国内的固定收益类回报基本上被压在接近于零的水平。除此之外，企业管理者基本上更愿意囤积现金、构建“懒惰”的资产负债表，而不是提高

turns.en: dividends or doing share buybacks or investing for future growth. Both of these equations have changed. The equity and the CEO's priority of taking care of shareholders as well, started about two and a half years ago. The big highlight of course were the reforms by the Tokyo Stock Exchange. If you run a company
turns.zh: 股息、进行股票回购（share buyback），或为未来增长而投资。这两个等式如今都变了。股权端，以及 CEO 们把照顾股东也当作优先事项，这大约始于两年半以前。最大的亮点当然是 Tokyo Stock Exchange 推行的改革。如果你经营一家公司，

turns.en: and your price to book is below one, we're going to shame you. And it did yield very positive results. The reality is that Japan's dividend yield, Japan's equity market dividend yield is now double of what it is on Wall Street. That just tells you that something has changed in terms of the income that you can earn from investing

turns.en: will not work. It never worked. Right? Well, the Japanese got it done. Right? And that was the situation then, to get out of deflation. turns.zh: 行不通。它从来就没行得通过。对吧？可日本人硬是把它做成了。对吧？那就是当时的局面——为了走出通缩。记住，Abe 上任时，通缩缺口、也就是产出缺口（output gap）、潜在 GDP 与实际 GDP 之间的缺口，大约在负 4% 左右。而今天，这个产出缺口

turns.zh: 真的有确凿证据吗？真的有那么多烟吗？是的，确实有通胀压力，但我们是否面临失控通胀的风险？我是说，这种风险当然不再为零了。对吧？但它仍然是可控的。我认为从这个角度看，尤其是 Ueda 行长，宁愿做一个循序渐进的渐进主义者，而不是

turns.zh: JGB 交易员，因为根本没有意义，日本央行会把任何发行的债券都吸走。由于收益率曲线控制，根本不存在市场。所以，重新注入流动性、或者我所说的把政府债务市场“重新私有化”，是 Ueda 行长想做的第一步。你可以证明

turns.en: (and the Bank of Japan publishes data on this) that when Governor Kuroda took over, less than 20% of the liquidity was from the private sector, the rest was all the Bank of Japan. Now we're back to 80%, 85%, 90% of the liquidity actually coming from the private sector. Every bank in Japan has hired JGB teams. They've
turns.zh: （日本央行还就此公布了数据）：当 Kuroda 行长接任时，来自私人部门的流动性不到 20%，其余全都是日本央行提供的。如今我们回到了 80%、85%、90% 的流动性实际上来自私人部门。日本的每家银行都组建了 JGB 团队。他们
